content: Pertussis, commonly referred to as whooping cough, is a highly contagious respiratory illness caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis. This disease is characterized by severe, uncontrollable coughing fits that can make it difficult to breathe. While pertussis can affect individuals of all ages, it poses a particularly serious, and sometimes fatal, risk to infants under one year of age. The bacteria are transmitted from person to person through respiratory droplets, such as those produced by coughing, sneezing, or close contact in shared breathing spaces. In the early stages, pertussis symptoms are mild and resemble those of a common cold. These symptoms may include a runny nose, a low-grade fever, and a mild cough. As the disease progresses, more severe symptoms develop, including episodes of rapid, consecutive coughing followed by a high-pitched whooping sound during inhalation. These coughing fits may also lead to vomiting and extreme fatigue. In infants, the characteristic cough may be absent, but they may experience pauses in breathing, known as apnea. The coughing episodes can persist for 10 weeks or longer, earning pertussis the nickname the 100-day cough. Globally, pertussis is a widespread disease, with higher prevalence in developing countries where vaccination rates are low. Each year, approximately 24.1 million cases of pertussis occur worldwide, resulting in an estimated 160,700 deaths among children under the age of five. Vaccination is the most effective method of preventing pertussis. The vaccines used to protect against pertussis are combination vaccines that also provide immunity against diphtheria and tetanus. These vaccines are commonly referred to as DTaP (for infants and young children) and Tdap (for older children, adolescents, and adults). For infants and young children, the CDC recommends a series of three DTaP doses at 2 months, 4 months, and 6 months of age, followed by two booster doses at 15–18 months and 4–6 years of age. Preteens should receive a single dose of Tdap between the ages of 11 and 12 to boost their immunity. Adolescents who missed the Tdap vaccine during their preteen years should receive it at their next healthcare visit. Pregnant women are advised to receive a Tdap vaccine during the early part of the third trimester of each pregnancy. This practice helps protect newborns from pertussis during their first few months of life, when they are most vulnerable and too young to be vaccinated themselves. Adults who have never received a Tdap vaccine should get one dose at any time, regardless of when they last received a tetanus or diphtheria vaccine. After this initial dose, adults should continue to receive either a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years to maintain immunity.
